# Mandhātujātaka (Ja 258)
**ID:** Ja 258
**Section:** Jātaka (ja)
**Collection:** Suttas-Late-1
**Title (Pali):** Mandhātujātaka
**SuttaCentral:** https://suttacentral.net/ja258

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
The *Mandhātujātaka* (Ja 258) is a narrative in the Pali Jātaka collection recounting the former life of the Buddha as the wheel-turning monarch (*cakkavatti*) Mandhātā [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1879]. The narrative framework opens at Jetavana, where the Buddha delivers the story concerning a backsliding monk (*ukkaṇṭhitabhikkhu*) who became infatuated with a woman while seeking alms in Sāvatthī [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1879]. In the *Dhammapada-aṭṭhakathā*, the story is similarly recounted to counsel a monk who became discontented after receiving an inheritance of money [Burlingame 1921]. In the past story, King Mandhātā was endowed with the seven precious treasures and supernormal faculties, capable of causing a knee-deep shower of gems by touching his clenched hands [Cueppers et al. 2010]. Having ruled the human realm for ages, he ascended to the heaven of the Thirty-Three to share the celestial throne with Sakka; however, driven by insatiable desire, he coveted sole rule and plotted to kill the king of gods [Meisig 2010]. His greed broke his supernormal lifespan, causing him to plunge back to earth, where he expired on a couch in his royal park after admonishing his people on the emptiness of worldly desires [Bapat 1956; Meisig 2010]. The Buddha concludes by identifying himself as King Mandhātā [Fausböll 1879].
The gāthās of the jātaka (opening with *Yāvatā candimasūriyā*) observe that even a rain of gold cannot satisfy sensual desires, concluding that the disciple of the Buddha delights in the cessation of craving (*appassādā dukhā kāmā ... taṇhakkhayarato*) [Fausböll 1879]. These verses correspond to canonical *Dhammapada* vv. 186–187 [SuttaCentral; DharmaNexus]. Curated parallels and machine alignments attest to extensive transmission across Buddhist traditions: parallel verse and narrative cycles appear in the Patna Dharmapada (*Taṇhavagga*), the *Udānavarga* (ch. 2, *Kāmavarga*), Chinese translations (T 210, T 212, T 213), the *Madhyama Āgama* (MĀ 60), the Sanskrit *Divyāvadāna* (ch. 17, *Māndhātāvadāna*), and the Mūlasarvāstivāda *Bhaiṣajyavastu* [SuttaCentral; DharmaNexus; Bingenheimer et al. 2013; Meisig 2010]. DharmaNexus identifies significant cross-language alignment between Ja 258 and the *Divyāvadāna*, alongside Pali text reuse with the *Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā* and the *Dhammapada-aṭṭhakathā* [DharmaNexus]. In Buddhist art, the story of King Mandhātā was frequently depicted in Andhra relief sculptures (Amarāvatī, Jaggayyapeta, Goli, and Nāgārjunakoṇḍa), Kanaganahalli, and later Burmese pagodas [Bapat 1956; Coomaraswamy 1935; Francis 2002; Shyu 2008; Zin].

- Resembling parallels (SuttaCentral): san-mu-kd6 Bhaiṣajyavastu; dhp186-187; SN 4.20 Rajjasutta; SN 4.21 Sambahulasutta
